kcet|Physics|2009|9|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
A star's surface temperature is read from the **colour** of its light — the wavelength at
which it shines most brightly — and that is **Wien's displacement law**.
**The law.**
**λ_max T = b**, with b = 2·898 × 10⁻³ m K
So measuring the wavelength of peak emission gives the temperature directly:
**T = b/λ_max** ✓
**Worked examples.**
The Sun peaks at about **500 nm** (green-yellow), giving
T = 2·898 × 10⁻³/(500 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ **5800 K** ✓
A red star peaking at **1000 nm** would be about **2900 K** — cooler
A blue star peaking at **290 nm** would be about **10000 K** — hotter ✓
This is why **blue stars are hot and red stars are cool**, the single most useful fact in
observational astronomy.
**Why the law applies to stars.** A star radiates very nearly as a **black body**, so its
spectrum follows the Planck curve, and that curve has a definite peak whose position
depends only on temperature ✓ No knowledge of the star's size or distance is needed —
which is essential, since both are hard to measure.
**Why not Planck's law.** Planck's law gives the **full** spectral distribution
E(λ, T), and it is the law from which Wien's is derived (by differentiating to find the
peak) ✗ It is correct but not what is **used** to extract a temperature from an
observation; one reads off the peak, not the whole curve.
**Why not the Rayleigh-Jeans law.** That is the **long-wavelength approximation** to
Planck's law, and it fails badly at short wavelengths — the "ultraviolet catastrophe" ✗
It has no peak at all, so it cannot give a temperature.
**Why not Kirchhoff's law.** Kirchhoff's law states that a good absorber is a good
emitter, e_λ/a_λ = E_λ ✗ It explains **why** stars behave as black bodies, but it
contains no temperature-wavelength relation.
**The distinction in one line.** Planck describes the whole curve, Rayleigh-Jeans one end
of it, Kirchhoff why the curve applies — and **Wien** locates its peak, which is what a
thermometer made of starlight needs ✓
∴ Wien's displacement law.
kcet|Physics|2013|11|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Carnot efficiency depends only on the **ratio** of the two absolute temperatures:
**η = 1 − T_sink/T_source**
so the efficiency is greatest where that ratio is **smallest**.
**Step 1 — compute each ratio and efficiency.**
**600 K, 400 K:** 400/600 = 0·667, so η = **33·3%**
**400 K, 200 K:** 200/400 = 0·500, so η = **50·0%**
**500 K, 300 K:** 300/500 = 0·600, so η = **40·0%**
**300 K, 100 K:** 100/300 = 0·333, so η = **66·7%** ✓ **the largest**
**Step 2 — conclude.** The combination **300 K, 100 K** gives the maximum efficiency ✓
**Why the ratio matters, not the difference.** Three of the four pairs differ by **200 K**
— 600/400, 500/300 and 300/100 — yet their efficiencies are 33%, 40% and 67% ✓ A fixed
temperature **gap** does not fix the efficiency; what counts is how large the sink
temperature is **relative to** the source.
**The pattern.** Among pairs with the same difference, the one with the **lower**
temperatures wins, because the same gap is then a larger fraction of the source
temperature ✓ Dropping from 300 K to 100 K discards two thirds of the absolute
temperature; dropping from 600 K to 400 K discards only one third.
**Why the temperatures must be absolute.** The formula is valid only in **kelvin** ✓ Using
Celsius would give nonsense — for the last pair, 1 − (−173)/27 is meaningless. All four
options are already in kelvin, which is the question's way of removing that trap.
**A practical note.** A real engine at 300 K source and 100 K sink would be a
**cryogenic** device, not a power station — the high efficiency comes from an extremely
cold sink, which costs energy to maintain. Actual power stations run near 800 K and 300 K,
giving a Carnot limit of about 62% and real efficiencies near 40% ✓
**Reading the distractors.** Each is a plausible pair, and the only way through is to
evaluate all four ✓ The arithmetic is quick since each ratio is a simple fraction:
2/3, 1/2, 3/5 and **1/3** — and the smallest ratio, 1/3, gives the largest efficiency.
∴ 300 K, 100 K.
kcet|Physics|2014|12|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Rearrange the Carnot efficiency formula for the source temperature, taking care to work
in **kelvin** and convert back at the end.
**Step 1 — convert the sink temperature to kelvin.**
T₂ = 27°C = 27 + 273 = **300 K**
**Step 2 — write the efficiency.**
η = 1 − T₂/T₁
**0·70 = 1 − 300/T₁**
**Step 3 — solve for T₁.**
300/T₁ = 1 − 0·70 = **0·30**
T₁ = 300/0·30 = **1000 K**
**Step 4 — convert back to Celsius**, since the options are in °C:
T₁ = 1000 − 273 = **727°C** ✓
**Check.** With T₁ = 1000 K and T₂ = 300 K:
η = 1 − 300/1000 = 1 − 0·3 = **0·70 = 70%** ✓
**The two conversions are the whole question.** The formula demands **absolute**
temperatures, so the sink must be turned into kelvin **before** use, and the answer turned
back into Celsius **after** ✓ Skipping either produces one of the distractors:
**1000°C** ✗ is the kelvin answer left unconverted — the commonest error, and it is
offered precisely for that.
**270°C** ✗ comes from using 27°C directly in the formula: 0·7 = 1 − 27/T₁ gives T₁ = 90,
and various mishandlings of that give 270 or 90.
**90°C** ✗ is that same mistake carried through.
**A sanity check on the size.** An efficiency of 70% needs the sink to be only **30%** of
the source temperature in kelvin ✓ With a sink at 300 K the source must be about
**three and a third times** hotter, that is around 1000 K — comfortably above 727°C in
Celsius terms, and far above anything one would reach by arithmetic on 27 alone.
**A practical note.** 727°C is attainable in a furnace, so the engine is not fanciful —
but no real engine reaches the Carnot limit, because that requires every step to be
**reversible** and infinitely slow ✓ 70% is the ceiling, not a working figure.
∴ 727°C.
kcet|Physics|2015|14|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Substitute directly into the Carnot efficiency formula; both temperatures are already in
**kelvin**.
**Step 1 — write the formula.**
**η = 1 − T₂/T₁**
with T₁ the source (hotter) and T₂ the sink (colder).
**Step 2 — substitute.** T₁ = 500 K and T₂ = 300 K:
η = 1 − 300/500
= 1 − 0·6
= **0·4**
**Step 3 — express as a percentage.**
0·4 × 100 = **40%** ✓
**An equivalent form.**
η = (T₁ − T₂)/T₁ = (500 − 300)/500 = 200/500 = **0·4** ✓ the same.
**Why the temperatures need no conversion.** They are given in **K** already ✓ Had they
been in Celsius, 500°C and 300°C would correspond to 773 K and 573 K, giving
1 − 573/773 = **25·9%** — a quite different answer, which is why option (a), 25%, is
offered as a trap for anyone who assumes Celsius.
**What the result means.** Of every 100 joules drawn from the 500 K reservoir, at most
**40 J** can become useful work; the remaining **60 J** must be dumped into the 300 K
sink ✓ That rejection is not a design flaw but a requirement of the second law — no engine
between these two temperatures can do better, however it is built.
**Reading the other distractors.**
**50%** ✗ would need T₂/T₁ = 0·5, that is a sink at 250 K.
**75%** ✗ would need a sink at 125 K.
Both require a colder sink than the 300 K given ✓ and since the efficiency rises only as
the sink falls, any answer above 40% is impossible here.
**A useful mental check.** The efficiency equals the **fraction of the source temperature
that is discarded**: from 500 K down to 300 K is a drop of 200, and 200/500 = **40%** ✓
That one-step reading avoids the formula entirely.
∴ 40%.
kcet|Physics|2019|3|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
The strong nuclear force has a range of only about **1 fm**, while 10 nm is **ten million
times** larger — so at that separation it has vanished entirely and only the
electromagnetic repulsion remains.
**Step 1 — compare the separation with the nuclear range.**
nuclear range ≈ 1 fm = **10⁻¹⁵ m**
given separation = 10 nm = **10⁻⁸ m**
ratio = 10⁻⁸/10⁻¹⁵ = **10⁷**
The protons are ten million nuclear diameters apart ✓
**Step 2 — recall how the nuclear force falls off.** It is **short-range**, dying away
roughly exponentially beyond a femtometre — not as an inverse square. Over 10⁷ ranges it
is utterly negligible:
**F_n ≈ 0** ✓
**Step 3 — compute the electromagnetic force**, which obeys the inverse-square law and so
is still perfectly measurable:
F_e = ke²/r²
= (9 × 10⁹)(1·6 × 10⁻¹⁹)²/(10⁻⁸)²
= (9 × 10⁹)(2·56 × 10⁻³⁸)/(10⁻¹⁶)
= **2·3 × 10⁻¹² N**
Small in absolute terms, but enormously larger than F_n ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.**
**F_e ≫ F_n** ✓
**The contrast with nuclear distances.** Inside a nucleus, where protons sit about
**1 fm** apart, the roles reverse completely: there the strong force is roughly **100
times** the electrostatic repulsion, which is exactly what holds the nucleus together ✓
So the same two protons give opposite answers at 1 fm and at 10 nm — and the whole
question is about reading the distance.
**Why the strong force must be short-range.** If it reached as far as electromagnetism,
all matter would collapse into a single nucleus ✓ Its abrupt cut-off is what allows atoms,
and chemistry, to exist at all.
**Reading the distractors.**
**F_e ≪ F_n** ✗ is the correct statement at **nuclear** separations, and it is the trap
for anyone who associates "two protons" with "nucleus" without checking the distance.
**F_e = F_n** ✗ and **they differ only slightly** ✗ would require the separation to sit in
the narrow crossover region near 1 fm, not seven orders of magnitude beyond it.
**A scale to hold on to.** 10 nm is about the width of a **cell membrane**, or a hundred
atoms side by side — vastly outside any nucleus ✓
∴ F_e ≫ F_n.
kcet|Physics|2015|10|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Write both quantities in base dimensions and divide.
**Step 1 — the dimensions of Planck's constant.** From E = hν,
h = E/ν = [ML²T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = **[ML²T⁻¹]**
(It is also the dimension of **angular momentum**, which is worth noting — and is why
option (d) is offered.)
**Step 2 — the dimensions of moment of inertia.** From I = mr²,
I = [M][L²] = **[ML²]**
**Step 3 — divide.**
h/I = [ML²T⁻¹]/[ML²]
= **[T⁻¹]**
the M and L² cancelling completely ✓
**Step 4 — identify the quantity.** [T⁻¹] is "per second" — the dimension of
**frequency** ✓
**A physical reading.** For a rotating body, angular momentum is L = Iω, so
ω = L/I. Since h has the dimensions of angular momentum, h/I has the dimensions of
**angular velocity**, and angular velocity shares its dimensions with frequency ✓ The
ratio is not a coincidence but the rotational analogue of velocity = momentum/mass.
**Checking the units numerically.**
h is in **J s = kg m² s⁻¹**
I is in **kg m²**
h/I is therefore in **s⁻¹** ✓ which is the hertz.
**Reading the distractors.**
**velocity** ✗ is [LT⁻¹] — it keeps a length, but the L² cancels exactly here.
**time** ✗ is [T], the **reciprocal** of the answer. It would be the dimension of I/h, and
it is the commonest error: dividing the wrong way round.
**angular momentum** ✗ is [ML²T⁻¹] — the dimension of **h itself**, not of the ratio.
Offered because h and angular momentum share dimensions, which is true but is a statement
about h alone.
**A caution about "dimensionless" quantities.** Angle is dimensionless, so angular
velocity (rad s⁻¹) and frequency (s⁻¹) have the **same** dimensions even though they are
physically distinct ✓ The question asks for the **dimension**, so frequency is the right
label.
∴ frequency.

kcet|Physics|2006|3|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch.s:
Read the **angular frequency** off the wave equation, then convert it to a period.
**Step 1 — expand the bracket.**
y = 5 sin[(π/2)(100t − x)]
= 5 sin[**50πt** − (π/2)x]
**Step 2 — compare with the standard form** y = A sin(ωt − kx):
amplitude **A = 5 m**
angular frequency **ω = 50π rad s⁻¹**
wave number **k = π/2 rad m⁻¹**
**Step 3 — convert ω to the period.**
T = 2π/ω
= 2π/(50π)
= 2/50
= **0·04 s** ✓
**Check through the frequency.**
ν = ω/2π = 50π/2π = **25 Hz**
and T = 1/ν = 1/25 = **0·04 s** ✓
**The other wave quantities**, as a consistency check.
wavelength: λ = 2π/k = 2π/(π/2) = **4 m**
speed: v = ω/k = 50π/(π/2) = **100 m s⁻¹**
and v = νλ = 25 × 4 = **100 m s⁻¹** ✓ the three agree, confirming ω was read correctly.
(The 100 appearing as the wave speed is no accident: in the form sin[c(100t − x)] the
coefficient of t inside the bracket **is** the speed, whatever c may be.)
**The step most easily missed.** The π/2 outside the bracket multiplies **both** terms, so
the coefficient of t is (π/2)(100) = **50π**, not 100 ✓ Taking ω = 100 would give
T = 2π/100 = 0·0628 s, which is not among the options — a sign that the bracket must be
expanded first.
**Reading the distractors.**
**0·01 s** ✗ corresponds to ω = 200π, that is doubling instead of halving the 100.
**1 s** ✗ would need ω = 2π, so the coefficient of t inside the sine would have to be 2π.
**5 s** ✗ is the **amplitude** in metres, not a time at all.
∴ 0·04.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, 1 second. Expanding the bracket gives
ω = (π/2)(100) = 50π rad s⁻¹, so T = 2π/50π = 0·04 s, confirmed by ν = 25 Hz and by the
consistency of λ = 4 m with v = 100 m s⁻¹. The key has been corrected to the first
option.
